  "text": "At morning service Tobias left room beside him. He put his hat on his knees instead of on the pew, though Maren had not sat there for years.

The minister had trouble with the latch of the little door behind the pulpit. Twice during the lesson it opened. The third time he left it and went on reading.

Afterward Tobias took the road above the dunes.

Her house was shut. The lamp stood unlit in the front window. From the gate he could see the chip in its base, a small white place he had never noticed before.

He called her name once. It sounded sufficient until he had finished saying it.

The eleven posts ran down beside the path. He counted them without moving his lips. Nothing hung from any of them. On the lowest step lay a little sand, combed into ridges, already drying.

Tobias had brought bread from the church kitchen. He had wrapped it while it was warm, and the paper had softened against his palm. He set it by the door, then picked it up again. There were birds about this morning.

He tried the latch.

It lifted easily. That was all. He held it raised a moment, with his shoulder drawn back from the wood, and let it fall.

In the end he hung the bread from the porch rail by its string.

All the way home he kept remembering that she would need scissors. He had tied the knot too tightly. His fingers had been cold.",

  "text": "In the morning the cloth beneath the plate was dry. Tobias lifted one corner and felt the table. That was dry too.

The loaf had split along its underside. He could see the close, grey crumb where the crust had drawn back. He put the kettle on and stood with his hands against the stove until the iron grew too warm.

On Wednesdays the fish cart came up from the landing. He heard its wheel strike the loose stone outside and waited for the usual second knock. The boy had learned to give him time.

When Tobias opened the door, the boy was looking toward the kitchen.

“Nothing today,” Tobias said.

The boy nodded. There was a scale on his cheek, just below one eye. Tobias almost told him.

After the cart had gone, he found a clean sheet of paper and wrapped the loaf. He carried it down to the shore by the long way, avoiding the upper road.

The tide was out. Between the stones lay ropes of weed and the white inside of a broken cup.

He unwrapped the bread above the tide line. There were gulls on the harbour wall, but none came down.

He waited, holding the paper by its dry corners.

At last he folded it and put it in his pocket. On his way back he stopped at the baker's. When she reached for the usual loaf, he asked for the smaller one.

She set it on the counter between them.

“Will that be enough?”
